A good final-year IoT project is not the one with the most sensors. It is one that solves a clearly stated problem, makes a measurable improvement over a simple baseline, and is evaluated honestly. Examiners and interviewers have seen many "smart home with an app" projects. What stands out is a project that asks a real question, such as "can a cheap sensor network detect a leak faster than a monthly meter reading?", and answers it with data.

This guide gives 30 IoT project ideas for final-year engineering students (electronics, electrical, computer science, instrumentation and mechanical), grouped into six areas. Each idea lists the problem, the system you would build, what makes it more than a demo, and how to evaluate it. Before the list, there is a short guide to choosing and scoping a project, and after it, a plan, a report structure and the mistakes that cost marks.

How we wrote this. Standards, datasets and platform facts are linked to their official sources, checked on 3 November 2026. The ideas are our own synthesis of common capstone themes and current technology. We do not claim any idea is unpublished; part of your work is a literature search to find what others have done and what you can add.

How to choose a final-year IoT project

Score each candidate idea from 1 to 5 on these questions, and pick one with a high total:

  1. Is the problem real? Can you name who has it and what it costs them (time, water, energy, safety)?
  2. Is there a baseline? "Better than a timer", "faster than a manual check" or "more accurate than a single uncalibrated sensor" gives you something to measure against.
  3. Can you get data? Either from your own deployment over several weeks, or from a public dataset, or both.
  4. Is it feasible in your time and budget? Parts available locally, a team member who can solder, access to a test site.
  5. Is there an engineering depth? Signal processing, control, networking, machine learning, power design or security, not just wiring modules together.
  6. Is it safe and ethical? No mains wiring by students without supervision, no medical claims, consent for any data about people.

Scope it down. A focused project that works and is evaluated beats an ambitious one that half works. A useful pattern: one sensing node + one gateway + one dashboard + one evaluation experiment, then add features only if time allows.

Choose the stack early:

  • Microcontroller nodes: ESP32 family boards are the default choice for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth; the ESP32-C6 and C5 add Thread and Zigbee radios for Matter work (Espressif).
  • Gateway or edge computer: Raspberry Pi or an old laptop or mini PC. Pi prices for larger-memory models have risen several times since late 2025 (Raspberry Pi), so check whether the cheaper 1 GB or 2 GB model is enough.
  • Messaging: MQTT through Mosquitto for most projects; LoRaWAN for long range and low power; Matter when interoperability with commercial smart home ecosystems is the point.
  • Storage and dashboards: InfluxDB or PostgreSQL with Grafana, or Node-RED for quick flows.

Agriculture and environment (ideas 1–5)

1. Evapotranspiration-based precision irrigation

Problem: timer-based irrigation wastes water on cool, humid days and under-waters during heat waves. System: soil moisture nodes plus a small weather station; the controller estimates crop water need with the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56) and waters only the deficit. Beyond a demo: compare against a fixed timer on two identical plots or pots. Evaluate: litres used per plot, soil moisture kept within target band (% of time), plant growth if the timeline allows.

2. Crop disease early warning

Problem: many fungal diseases develop when leaves stay wet at certain temperatures for long enough. System: leaf wetness, temperature and humidity sensors feed a published disease-risk model for a local crop; optionally an ESP32-S3 camera with a small image classifier flags visible symptoms. Beyond a demo: justify the risk model from agricultural literature and work with a local farm or agricultural department. Evaluate: agreement between your risk alerts and expert field observations; for the classifier, precision and recall on a held-out image set.

3. Calibrated low-cost air quality network

Problem: low-cost particulate sensors are inexpensive enough to deploy widely but can be biased, especially in high humidity. System: several PM2.5 nodes, one placed next to an official reference monitor (co-location), and a calibration model (for example linear regression with a humidity term) applied to the rest. The U.S. EPA's Air Sensor Toolbox explains co-location and performance targets. Beyond a demo: the calibration study itself is the research contribution. Evaluate: error (RMSE, R²) against the reference before and after calibration, and data completeness.

4. Flood and river level early warning

Problem: small streams and drains can rise quickly, and communities often get little warning. System: ultrasonic or pressure level sensors on LoRaWAN nodes along a channel, sending to a gateway that issues alerts on rate of rise, not only on level. Beyond a demo: detection based on rate of rise and upstream readings gives earlier warnings than a single threshold. Evaluate: detection lead time in a controlled test (a tank or channel you fill), false alarm rate, battery life and packet delivery ratio. Respect radio duty-cycle rules and network fair-use limits (The Things Network).

5. Smart beehive monitor

Problem: beekeepers open hives to check them, which disturbs the colony, and swarming or starvation can go unnoticed. System: a load cell under the hive for weight, internal temperature and humidity, and a microphone whose sound spectrum (computed on the device) may indicate swarming behaviour. Beyond a demo: sound features plus weight trends; work with a local beekeeper. Evaluate: weight measurement accuracy against reference weights, correlation of alerts with the beekeeper's records.

Health, safety and assistive technology (ideas 6–10)

These ideas involve people. Do not describe any of them as diagnosing or treating a condition; that would make them medical devices, which are regulated. Frame them as wellness, assistive or alerting prototypes, and get ethics approval and written consent before collecting data from people.

6. Fall detection wearable with on-device machine learning

Problem: older adults who fall may be unable to call for help. System: an accelerometer and gyroscope on a wrist or waist node, with a small classifier running on the microcontroller and a BLE or Wi-Fi alert. Data: public fall datasets such as SisFall for training, plus your own simulated falls onto mats. Evaluate: sensitivity and specificity, and especially false alarms per day of normal wear, which decides whether people would keep using it.

7. Smart pillbox for medication adherence

Problem: missed doses are common with complex medication schedules. System: compartment lid sensors (reed switches or light sensors), reminders with light and sound, and a caregiver alert if a dose is missed. Beyond a demo: design for the user: large buttons, clear feedback, and an offline mode when Wi-Fi fails. Evaluate: detection accuracy of lid events, a usability test with volunteers (with consent), and alert delivery time.

8. Obstacle-sensing aid for people with visual impairment

Problem: a white cane does not detect obstacles at head height. System: time-of-flight or ultrasonic sensors on a cane or wearable, with vibration feedback whose intensity increases as obstacles get closer. Beyond a demo: co-design with users or an organisation for blind people; their feedback is worth more than extra sensors. Evaluate: detection range and angle, false positives in a corridor course, battery life.

9. Contactless breathing and sleep monitoring (wellness)

Problem: wearable sleep trackers are uncomfortable for some people. System: a 60 GHz or 24 GHz mmWave radar module next to the bed estimates movement and breathing rate without a camera. Evaluate: breathing rate against a manual count or a chest strap reference, and robustness to a second person in the bed. Present it as a wellness and research prototype only.

10. Cold-chain monitor for medicines in transit

Problem: temperature-sensitive medicines and vaccines can be damaged during transport without anyone knowing. System: a battery-powered node with a temperature probe, GPS, cellular or LoRaWAN connectivity, and a tamper-evident log: each record includes a hash of the previous one so edits can be detected. Evaluate: temperature accuracy against a calibrated thermometer, battery life over a trip, and how well the system handles areas with no coverage (store and forward).

Smart energy (ideas 11–15)

11. Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM)

Problem: households see one total on the bill but not which appliance uses what. System: measure whole-house or whole-room power at high resolution and use algorithms to separate (disaggregate) individual appliances. Data: public datasets such as UK-DALE and REDD for training and comparison, plus your own measurements from a supervised setup using plug-in meters as ground truth. Evaluate: per-appliance energy error and event detection F1 score. This is a strong project for students who like signal processing and machine learning.

12. Solar panel performance and soiling detection

Problem: dust and partial shading reduce solar output, and owners often do not notice. System: measure panel output alongside irradiance (a reference cell or a clean small panel) and temperature; compare actual output with expected output and alert when the ratio drops. Evaluate: detection of a known soiling or shading event you create, and the energy recovered after cleaning.

13. Smart EV or e-bike charging scheduler

Problem: charging at peak times costs more and strains the grid. System: a controller that schedules charging using a time-of-use tariff and a solar forecast. For real chargers, study the Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) used between chargers and management systems (Open Charge Alliance); for a safe student build, control a low-voltage e-bike charger through a certified smart plug. Evaluate: cost and share of solar energy compared with "charge on arrival".

14. Occupancy-based classroom HVAC and lighting

Problem: lights and air conditioning run in empty rooms. System: CO₂, PIR and mmWave sensors estimate occupancy; the controller adjusts lights and AC setpoints through IR or building interfaces. Evaluate: energy saved over matched weeks, comfort (temperature and CO₂ within limits), and occupancy estimation accuracy against manual counts.

15. Battery state-of-health monitor

Problem: batteries in UPS units, e-bikes and solar systems degrade silently until they fail. System: measure voltage, current and temperature; estimate state of charge by coulomb counting and track capacity fade and internal resistance over cycles. Safety: lithium cells can catch fire. Use a commercial battery management system, a fireproof test area and supervision. Evaluate: state-of-charge error against a full controlled discharge, and the trend in estimated capacity.

Smart cities and transport (ideas 16–20)

16. Smart parking occupancy

Problem: drivers waste time and fuel circling for parking. System: a magnetometer or time-of-flight sensor per bay on a low-power network, with a live map. Evaluate: occupancy detection accuracy over several days, battery life projection and the effect of weather.

17. Campus bus arrival prediction

Problem: students wait at stops not knowing when the bus will come. System: GPS trackers on buses, a server that predicts arrival times from historical travel times, and a web display. Evaluate: mean absolute error of arrival predictions against actual arrivals, compared with the timetable as a baseline.

18. Waste bin fill monitoring and route optimisation

Problem: bins are emptied on fixed schedules whether full or not. System: ultrasonic fill-level sensors on bins, and a route planner that visits only bins above a threshold (a vehicle routing problem). Evaluate: distance and number of stops saved versus the fixed route in a simulation using your measured fill rates. Our mathematical optimization techniques guide covers the optimisation side.

19. Privacy-preserving noise mapping

Problem: noise pollution affects health, but data is sparse. System: microphone nodes compute sound levels (for example A-weighted equivalent level) on the device and send only the numbers, never audio. Beyond a demo: calibrate against a sound level meter, and show that no audio leaves the device. Evaluate: error against the meter, and a map of levels by time of day.

20. Structural health monitoring of a model bridge

Problem: damage changes a structure's natural vibration frequencies. System: accelerometer nodes with time synchronisation on a lab-scale bridge or frame; compute natural frequencies by FFT and detect shifts when you add mass or loosen a joint. Evaluate: frequency estimation accuracy against a reference (a wired data acquisition system or simulation) and the smallest detectable change. Never install sensors on a public structure without the owner's permission.

Industrial IoT and safety (ideas 21–25)

21. Predictive maintenance for small motors

Problem: unplanned motor failures stop production. System: vibration and current sensing on a motor test rig, features computed on the edge, and an anomaly-detection model. Data: start with labelled bearing faults from the CWRU Bearing Data Center, then test on your own rig with induced faults such as imbalance (a small added weight). Evaluate: detection rate and false alarms; time between anomaly detection and a defined failure threshold.

22. Gas leak detection with automatic ventilation

Problem: LPG and natural gas leaks in kitchens and labs are dangerous. System: a gas sensor node that triggers an exhaust fan and an alarm, and sends a remote alert. Safety: low-cost MQ-series sensors are not certified safety devices. Your prototype must sit alongside, never replace, a certified detector. Test with safe calibration gas under supervision, not by releasing fuel. Evaluate: response time to a calibrated test gas, false alarms from cooking, and alert delivery time.

23. Digital twin of a small process

Problem: operators need to test changes without risking the real process. System: a lab process (a water tank with pump and valve, or a small conveyor) instrumented with sensors; data streams over MQTT or OPC UA, the widely used industrial interoperability standard (OPC Foundation), to a simulation model that runs in parallel and predicts behaviour. Evaluate: prediction error of the twin against the real process, and a demonstration of a "what if" test that was done on the twin first.

24. Heat stress monitoring for outdoor workers

Problem: heat illness is a serious risk for construction and farm workers. System: a site station measuring temperature, humidity, solar radiation and wind to estimate a heat stress index, with alerts for rest breaks; optional wearable nodes. Evaluate: index accuracy against a reference instrument or published calculations, and alert timeliness. Follow your local occupational health guidance for thresholds rather than inventing your own.

25. Machine utilisation (OEE) for a workshop

Problem: small workshops do not know how much of the time their machines are actually running. System: non-invasive current clamps (fitted by a qualified electrician) detect run, idle and off states; a dashboard computes availability and utilisation. Evaluate: state detection accuracy against video or manual logs, and insights you can show the workshop.

Security, networking and edge AI (ideas 26–30)

26. Intrusion detection for IoT networks

Problem: IoT devices are common targets for botnets. System: a Raspberry Pi gateway captures network flow features and a machine learning model flags attacks. Data: public IoT security datasets such as CICIoT2023 and TON_IoT, then your own lab traffic. Evaluate: precision, recall and false positive rate per attack type, and latency on the Pi. Only run attack traffic on your own isolated lab network.

27. Secure firmware update pipeline

Problem: many IoT devices never get security updates, or accept any firmware they are sent. System: ESP32 devices with secure boot and flash encryption enabled (Espressif Secure Boot v2), signed over-the-air updates, version checks and automatic rollback. Why now: regulation is pushing in this direction. The EU Cyber Resilience Act sets security requirements for products with digital elements, with obligations phasing in from 2026 to 2027 (European Commission), and consumer IoT baselines such as ETSI EN 303 645 ask for secure updates. Evaluate: demonstrate that unsigned or tampered firmware is rejected, measure update time and show rollback after a deliberately broken update. Practise on spare boards: enabling secure boot and flash encryption can be irreversible.

28. Privacy-preserving people counting with edge vision

Problem: libraries, canteens and buses want occupancy data, but people object to cameras sending video. System: a camera board (ESP32-S3 or a Raspberry Pi with an AI accelerator) counts people on the device and sends only counts; no images are stored or transmitted. Evaluate: counting accuracy against manual counts, frames per second, and an audit showing no image data leaves the device. Post clear notices and follow your institution's rules.

29. Matter and Thread interoperability testbed

Problem: smart home buyers face competing standards, and performance claims are rarely measured. System: the same sensor and light built for Wi-Fi, Zigbee and Thread/Matter (ESP32-C6 boards support all three radios), controlled through Home Assistant and at least one commercial ecosystem. The CSA released Matter 1.5 in November 2025 (CSA). Evaluate: command latency, reliability over a week, battery life for each protocol and the setup steps a user needs.

30. Federated learning across IoT nodes

Problem: sending raw sensor data to a central server costs bandwidth and can expose private data. System: several Raspberry Pi edge nodes train a shared anomaly-detection or activity-recognition model with federated learning, where only model updates leave each node, using a framework such as Flower. Evaluate: model accuracy compared with centralised training, bytes transmitted, and the effect of nodes with very different data.

A two-semester plan

Phase Weeks Output
Problem and literature review 1–4 Problem statement, 15–25 relevant papers, baseline defined
Requirements and design 5–7 Block diagram, parts list and budget, evaluation plan
Prototype one node end to end 8–12 Sensor → node → gateway → dashboard working
Mid-term review 13 Demo and revised plan
Build out and harden 14–20 All nodes, enclosures, power, security basics
Deployment and data collection 21–26 At least 2–4 weeks of data, or controlled experiments
Analysis and report 27–32 Results against baseline, report, poster, demo video

Order the parts in week 5. Delivery delays and dead modules are among the most common reasons projects slip, so buy spares of cheap sensors.

What to put in the report

  1. Abstract: problem, approach, key result with a number.
  2. Introduction: who has the problem and why it matters.
  3. Literature review: what exists, what is missing, where your work fits. Use IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar and arXiv, and cite what you actually read.
  4. System design: architecture diagram, hardware, firmware, network, data flow, and why you made each choice.
  5. Implementation: circuits, code structure, calibration procedures.
  6. Evaluation: method, metrics, baseline, results with charts and error bars, and statistical caution about small samples.
  7. Limitations and ethics: what does not work, safety, privacy and data protection (for example the GDPR in Europe or India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, depending on where you are).
  8. Conclusion and future work.
  9. Appendices: schematics, bill of materials with costs, code repository link.

Our machine learning projects and data analysis projects guides help with the evaluation chapter, and how to read engineering blog posts critically helps with judging sources in the literature review.

Mistakes that cost marks

  • No baseline. "It works" is not a result. Compare against something.
  • No calibration. Low-cost sensors need checking against a reference.
  • Too little data. One afternoon of readings cannot support claims about reliability.
  • Claiming accuracy you did not measure. Quote datasheet figures as datasheet figures.
  • Medical or safety claims. Never say your prototype diagnoses, prevents or protects; say it estimates, monitors or alerts, and state its limits.
  • Hardcoded passwords and open ports. Examiners increasingly ask about security; show you thought about it.
  • A demo that only works on campus Wi-Fi at your desk. Test on battery, in the real location, after a reboot.
